slides.title: The big idea: tokens read each other
slides.summary: Attention lets each token pick up information from the other tokens it needs, so words get their meaning from the words around them.
body: After the lookup step, each token's vector knows nothing about its neighbours. "Bank" has the same vector in "river bank" and "bank account". To understand text, a token has to look at the words around it.
Attention is how it does that. Each token builds a new vector that takes its context into account, by pulling in information from the other tokens that matter to it.

body.h: A question, a name tag and a backpack

body: Every token brings three things:

ul: Query, a question ❓: what this token needs to find out. “it” asks: who am I talking about?
Key, a name tag 🏷: what this token is, so others can find it. “cat” says: an animal.
Value, a backpack 🎒: what this token knows and hands over if it's picked.

body: Each token checks its question against every other token's name tag. <mark>The better a name tag fits, the more the token takes from that token's backpack.</mark>

body.note: Why keep key and value separate? Because what you match on isn't what you get back. Like a search engine: you match on keywords, but you read the page.

body: The next four slides follow “it” in “The cat sat on the mat because it” step by step. Each one also shows the maths on a tiny example, if you want it.

body.text: For a longer, step-by-step walkthrough of how attention works, read Attention, on learn.ratishfolio.com.

figure.alt: Each token vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to make queries, keys and values. Every query is compared with every key to give a grid of scores. Scores for future tokens are masked out. Softmax turns each row into weights that add up to 1, for example "artificial" puts 36 percent of its weight on "learning". Each token's output is the weighted mix of the value vectors.
figure.caption: The map for this chapter. The next four slides walk through each step.

slides.title: Step 1: a question, a name tag and a backpack
slides.summary: Three learned transforms turn each token into a query, a key and a value.
body: Every token goes through three learned transforms, W_Q, W_K and W_V. Think of them as three functions, to_query, to_key and to_value. The same three run on every token.

ul: Query ❓: “it” asks: who am I talking about? Probably something earlier, and alive.
Key 🏷: “cat” is labelled an animal, “mat” an object, “sat” an action.
Value 🎒: what “cat” hands over: an animal, furry, the one that sat down.

body: <mark>Nobody writes these transforms. Training tunes them until the right questions find the right name tags.</mark>

body.note: Learned in training: only the three tables, W_Q, W_K and W_V, one set per head in every layer. They're fixed afterwards. Worked out every time you send text: each token's query, key and value vectors, by multiplying the token's vector by those tables.

body: In GPT-2, each table is 768 × 64. 768 is the model's width: the size of every token's vector, the same as its embedding size, chosen by the designers before training. 64 is that width split across 12 heads (768 ÷ 12).

text: Each transform is a matrix multiplication: Q = x·W_Q, K = x·W_K, V = x·W_V, where x is the token's vector.

The tables on the right use a tiny example, “I am learning artificial”: each token has 4 numbers and each Q, K or V vector has 3. Real models use thousands, and 64–128 per head. Green cells are positive, red cells negative.

slides.title: How 768 numbers become 64
slides.summary: Multiplying a vector by a table: compare the vector with each column, and get one number per column.
body: Each of W_Q, W_K and W_V turns a token's 768 numbers into 64. Here's how that multiplication works, using nothing more than multiplying and adding.
(1 × 768) × (768 × 64) = (1 × 64). The inner sizes must match, and the outer sizes are what you get.

ul: The table has 64 columns, and each column is a list of 768 numbers, the same length as the token.
Lay the token's numbers against one column: multiply each pair, then add them all up. That gives one number.
Do it for all 64 columns, and you get 64 numbers out.

body: Each column is like one small question about the token, and the 64 answers make up its query, key or value for that head. Each answer is the same “do they line up?” comparison as the matching step: a dot product, done once per column.

body.text: All over the model. The MLP's first table is 768 × 3,072, so 768 numbers in and 3,072 out, one per detector. And the very last table turns 768 numbers into one score for every token in the vocabulary.

viz.html: Multiply the token by each column row by row, then add down the column: 2 and 3.

figure.alt: Left, the size rule: a 1 × 768 token times a 768 × 64 table gives a 1 × 64 result; the inner sizes must match and the outer sizes are what you get. Middle, a tiny example: the token [1, 0, 2, 1] next to a 4 × 2 table. Column 1 is [1, 0, 0, 1]; multiplying pair by pair and adding gives 1·1 + 0·0 + 2·0 + 1·1 = 2. Column 2 gives 3, so the result is [2, 3]: one number per column. Right, GPT-2, one head: 64 columns of 768 numbers each, so 64 comparisons and 64 numbers out; each column asks one small question about the token.
figure.caption: One number per column: that's all a vector-times-table multiplication is.

slides.title: Step 2: match every question against every name tag
slides.summary: Each token checks its question against the name tag of every token. The result is a grid of match scores.
body: “it” checks its question against every name tag. “cat” fits best, “mat” fits a little, and the rest hardly at all. Each check gives a score.

body.note: A query and a key are both lists of numbers. To check the fit, multiply them number by number and add up: a dot product. Say the query of “it” is [2, 1] (a noun, alive). Cat's key [1, 1] gives 2×1 + 1×1 = 3, a strong match. Mat's key [1, 0] gives 2×1 + 1×0 = 2, a weaker one.

body: Every token does this with every token, so the scores form a grid: one row for each token asking, one column for each name tag.

body.note: One score for every pair of tokens. <mark>Double the length of the text and you get four times the work.</mark> That's why long prompts are expensive.

text: The whole grid of scores is S = Q·Kᵀ: every query dotted with every key at once (Kᵀ is K flipped on its side so the multiplication lines up).
The scores are then divided by √d_head, here √3. Long vectors give big scores, and big scores would make the next step put almost all the weight on one token.
The grid on the right is for “I am learning artificial”. n tokens give n² scores: attention's O(n²) cost.

slides.title: Step 3: no peeking ahead
slides.summary: A mask stops each token from looking at later tokens. That's what makes next-token training work.
body: GPT, Claude, Llama and other chat models are decoder-only models, trained to predict the next token. If a token could see the one after it, predicting it would be too easy: the model would just copy the answer.

So every token can only look at the tokens before it, and itself. “it” can read “cat”'s name tag, but not the tag of whatever comes next. Scores for later tokens are blocked and count as zero. This is called the causal mask.

There's a big bonus. Since no token can see ahead, one pass over a training sentence trains every position at once: position 1 predicts token 2, position 2 predicts token 3, and so on, all at the same time.

Encoder models like BERT, used for sorting text into categories and for search, skip the mask and look both ways. That's great for understanding a finished sentence, but they can't write text one token at a time. Switch the mask on and off to compare.

body.text: Every score above the diagonal of the grid, where a token would look at a later one, is set to −∞ (minus infinity). In the next step, −∞ becomes exactly 0.

body.more: If “it” can't see “tired”, when is “it” resolved?
text: In “The cat sat on the mat, because it was tired”, “it” is processed before “tired” exists, so its own vector can't settle on the cat or the mat, and the mask means it never changes later.

The later words do the work instead. At “tired”, attention looks back at “it”, “cat” and “mat”, and layer by layer that position works out that the one who's tired is the cat. Every word after it can use that. In a look-both-ways model like BERT, “it” would see “tired” directly.

slides.title: Step 4: turn scores into shares, then blend the backpacks
slides.summary: Each row of scores becomes shares that add up to 100%. Each token then blends the values using those shares.
body: Each row of scores becomes attention weights: shares that add up to 100%. The best match gets the biggest share, but the others still get a little. This step is called softmax.
Then each token blends the backpacks using those shares. “it” takes mostly from “cat”'s backpack, a little from “mat”'s and almost nothing from the rest. Now “it” carries the meaning of the cat.

body.note: <mark>That's all attention is: ask a question, match it against every name tag, and blend the backpacks.</mark> The rest of this chapter is about doing it many times side by side, and doing it fast.

body: Pick a query row on the right to see where each token looks in the tiny example.

text: Softmax raises e (≈ 2.718) to the power of each score, then divides by the total. Scores [2, 1, 0] become e² ≈ 7.39, e¹ ≈ 2.72 and e⁰ = 1, which add up to 11.11, so the weights are 0.67, 0.24 and 0.09. A blocked score of −∞ becomes e−∞ = 0.
The output is a weighted sum of the value vectors: out = softmax(S)·V. If “artificial” puts 36% of its weight on “learning”, 36% of its new vector comes from the value of “learning”.

slides.title: Multi-head attention: many questions at once
slides.summary: Models run many attention heads side by side. Each head asks its own question, with its own name tags and backpacks.
body: One head asks one question. <mark>But a token often needs several answers at once.</mark>
So models run many attention heads side by side. Each head has its own three transforms, so in every head a token gets a different question, name tag and backpack. For “it”:

ul: Head 1 asks “who am I?” and takes from “cat”.
Head 2 asks “what did I do?” and takes from “sat”.
Head 3 asks “what came just before me?” and takes from “because”.

body: The heads' answers are joined, so “it” now knows it's the cat, that it sat, and what came just before.

body.note: Picture a team reading the same document, each person looking for something different, who then share their notes.

body: Researchers who look inside models find heads that specialise. The four patterns on the right are simplified versions of common ones. The first-token pattern is real and has a name, an attention sink: where heads put their weight when nothing else fits.

body.text: To keep the cost the same, each head uses smaller vectors: d_head = d_model / h. A model 4,096 numbers wide with 32 heads gives each head 128. The heads' outputs are joined end to end and mixed by one more learned matrix, W_O.

slides.title: Why attention is expensive
slides.summary: Attention's work grows with the square of the text length. That's why long prompts cost more.
body: Every token checks its question against the name tag of every token before it. With 10 words that's about 50 checks; with 20 words, about 200. Double the length of the text and the work goes up four times. Twice as many tokens are asking, and each has twice as many name tags to check. That's all n² means.
And it happens in every head, in every layer. Drag the slider to watch it grow.

body.note: This is why long prompts are slower and cost more. A 200,000-token prompt has 100 times the tokens of a 2,000-token one, but roughly 10,000 times the attention work.

body.more: How do models keep it under control?
text: FlashAttention gets exactly the same result, but works in small chunks that fit in the GPU's fast memory, so the full grid is never stored.
Grouped-query attention (GQA): several query heads share one set of name tags and backpacks, so the KV cache (next slide) gets several times smaller.
Sliding-window and sparse attention: some layers only look back a fixed distance, or at chosen positions.

body.text: For a closer look at how the KV cache works and what it costs, read KV cache, on learn.ratishfolio.com.

slides.title: Many layers, many heads, one KV cache each
slides.summary: Every layer runs many attention heads, and keeps a cache of past keys and values so each new token only does its own work.

ul: Past tokens don't change. A token can't look ahead, so the name tag (K) and backpack (V) of “cat” come out the same on every run.
So every layer saves them in its own KV cache: a K and a V for each earlier token, for every head.
Each new token does only its own work: it computes its Q, K and V, saves its K and V, and reuses everyone else's.

body: <mark>Thanks to the cache, each run after the first works on just one new token, which is why answers can stream out quickly.</mark>

body.note: Q isn't cached: only the newest token asks a question, and it asks once.

body.text: Memory. It grows with every token, in every layer. The table shows GPT-2's numbers; big models with long texts can need gigabytes, more than the model itself.
body.link: The KV cache, in Output & inference

body.more: How long is the cache kept?
text: During one request, it lives in GPU memory while the reply is being written, and is freed when the reply ends.
Across chat turns, each new message resends the whole conversation, so without prompt caching the cache is built again from scratch.

With prompt caching, providers keep the cache for a matching opening for a few minutes (around 5 by default, longer on request; check your provider's docs). Self-hosted servers such as vLLM keep it until GPU memory runs short.

figure.alt: An LLM as a stack of identical transformer layers, layer 1 up to layer N (12 in GPT-2). The tokens “The cat sat on the” enter at the bottom. Inside every layer, multi-head attention runs heads 1 to 12 side by side, each making its own Q, K and V, then a feed-forward network works on each token alone. Beside every layer is its own KV cache: a K row and a V row for every earlier token. The new token saves its K and V into the cache and reuses the stored ones; Q isn't cached. At the top, linear and softmax pick the next token, “mat”. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Many layers, many heads per layer, and a KV cache for each layer so past tokens are never worked out again.

slides.title: Position in depth: the wave pattern
slides.summary: Attention on its own ignores word order. The original Transformer fixed that with position vectors built from waves at different speeds.
body: Now you can see why attention needs position. Each token scores every other token with a dot product of a query and a key, and nothing in that calculation depends on where the tokens sit. Leave out the mask and shuffle the input, and every token gets the same scores, just in a different order.
Embeddings showed the fix: add a position vector to each token's vector. Here is how the original Transformer (2017) built those vectors.

ul: Each pair of numbers in the position vector follows a wave (a sine and a cosine) at its own speed, from very fast to very slow.
To get position 5's vector, read every wave at position 5. That is the stamp added to the token there.
Fast waves tell neighbours apart; slow waves tell near from far.

body: <mark>Every position gets a unique vector, nearby positions get similar ones, and every value stays between −1 and +1, so the position never drowns out the word.</mark>

body.note: Think of a clock with many hands. The second hand alone can't tell you the time. But seconds, minutes, hours and days together mark every moment uniquely, and moments close together look alike.

body.more: Why not just add the number 5?
body.text: Token vectors hold small numbers, roughly between −1 and +1. Adding 5,000 for a late position would swamp the word's meaning. Dividing by the text length instead would make position 5 mean different things in short and long texts. Waves avoid both, and need no training.

body: In the heatmap, each row is a position and each column one number: fast-changing columns on the left, slow ones on the right.

figure.alt: Why models need position, and how the original Transformer added it. First, without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" contain the same three tokens, so attention alone gives the same result for both. Second, with position, every token is stamped with its place in the sentence, 0, 1 or 2, so "dog at position 0" and "dog at position 2" become different inputs: the input is the token vector plus a position vector. Third, the position vector comes from waves at different speeds. Four waves are drawn across positions 0 to 16, from the fastest to the slowest. Reading all four waves at position 5 gives that position its own stamp: about −0.96, +0.60, +0.89 and +0.43. Nearby positions get similar stamps.
figure.caption: Without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same to attention. A position vector, read off waves at different speeds, stamps each token with where it sits.
